newsitem.title: GERMANY: Gloom, not celebrations, as Kohl breaks record.
newsitem.headline: Gloom, not celebrations, as Kohl breaks record.

text.p: Helmut Kohl on Thursday broke Konrad Adenauer's record to become Germany's longest-serving chancellor this century, but the political mood had more to do with belt-tightening and budget chaos than celebration.

Kohl himself had already opted to spend "K-Day" in Japan, far from bitter coalition wrangling, a crisis brewing over federal finances, and editorials saying the chancellor of 14 years and one month cannot avoid his share of responsibility.

Thursday's newspaper front pages dwelt above all on Finance Minister Theo Waigel's admission in an emergency parliamentary debate that his 1997 budget shortfall was even bigger than he had so far conceded.

An opinion poll by the Forsa research institute in Thursday's edition of the weekly Die Woche suggested that voters' were at last running out of confidence that Kohl was the man to see them through troubles.
For the first time since well before the elections of October 1994, the opposition centre-left Social Democrats (SPD) led Kohl's conservative Christian Democrats with 40 percent to 38.
The SPD and the environmentalist Greens together scored 50 percent, enough to form a coalition government if it had been an election vote.

Germans, and above all the increasingly restive workers, are getting frustrated with one government austerity measure after another chipping away at welfare benefits and pushing up taxes, with no end in sight.

On Tuesday leading economic institutes attacked government budget management and said on current showing Germany, normally a model of financial prudence, would not meet the criteria for its cherished project of a single European Union currency.
A few commentators were not surprised that Kohl, who skilfully orchestrated media coverage and launched a book in the run-up to his landmark date, was spending the day itself abroad.
"On the international stage, Kohl is highly regarded," WDR public television said in an editorial which saw the chancellor's main achievements as pushing German and European unity.
"At home his record after 14 years doesn't look so rosy. The laborious grind of home-made problems isn't really his thing."
Even conservative commentators accept that Kohl's survival has little to do with visionary policy.
"Kohl is not a jack-of-all-trades, he is a specialist in the art of achieving and holding on to power. That explains his success," said private RTL television.
With Kohl looking increasingly likely to lead his party through yet another election in 1998, doubts are starting to emerge whether this is what Germany needs in its current state.
The drawing together of divided Germany in 1990 is often seen as the achievement which transformed Kohl from an apparently bumbling provincial politician into Europe's leading statesman.

But critical voices are also starting to say that unification and the trillion-mark burden it imposed on western Germany were a huge missed opportunity to reform post-war structures which are holding back the economy, preventing job-creation and making the budget so hard to tame.

The liberal Sueddeutsche Zeitung said the government's determination to stick with Kohl could become a costly error if "word gets round that the chancellor was not and is not in any position to put in place a reform of his highly risky economic and financial policy following German unification".
Berlin's SFB radio said Kohl had had his eye on history for a long time: "That's certainly not reprehensible, but it's also not enough."
